collection_summary: Adapted / expanded from seed #4 in datasets/pkdb_bench/docs/example_questions.txt ('What are top 3 dishes that are high in vitamin C'). Expanded from one vitamin × top-3 dishes (3 rows — fails the 10-row viability gate) to six vitamins × five food sources (30 rows, viable). Cycle-0 staging applied all the cycles 1+2+3 lessons from prior scaled_enumeration instances: (a) selection framing ('notable' not 'top'); (b) PK = (Vitamin, Food) with List Position non-key; (c) per-row Wikipedia article cited from cycle 0. Cycle-1 audit added three further fixes: (d) B12 rows tightened to article-verbatim foods — replaced Clams (subspecific to 'shellfish') and Salmon (subspecific to 'fish') with Lamb liver and Turkey liver (named in the article quote 'organ meats from lamb, veal, beef, and turkey'); (e) K rows rebalanced from K2-only (cycle-0: Nattō, Egg yolk, Goose, Butter, Hard cheese — auditor flagged this as not spanning the broad K partition) to K1+K2 mix (cycle-1: Nattō K2 + Collard greens K1 + Spinach K1 + Kale K1 + Egg yolk K2); (f) secondary_category dropped from 'top_k' to '' because the framing is 'notable' selection (not ranked top-K) and B12/K rows are not clean content rankings. Tier B (manual_wikipedia) extraction. Universe is 6 vitamins (A, B12, C, D, E, K) anchored to Wikipedia 'Vitamin' which lists 13 essential vitamins; the staged 6 span the classification (4 fat-soluble: A, D, E, K + 1 B-complex representative: B12 + the standalone water-soluble: C). Per-vitamin 5-food-source listings come from each per-vitamin Wikipedia article's Sources section. Result: 6 vitamins x 5 food sources = 30 rows x 5 columns, composite PK on (Vitamin, Food), 0 duplicate PKs. Multi-attribute (Approximate Content + Source Type) over the per-vitamin partition exercises the calibration goal of scaled_enumeration: well-known nutrition associations (Vitamin C → citrus fruits / acerola; Vitamin A → liver / carrots; Vitamin K → leafy greens / nattō) are very strong recall signals, while specific food rankings within a vitamin (Kakadu plum > Camu camu > Acerola for Vitamin C) progressively exercise the confidence gradient. Source Type column adds a categorical attribute that an LLM should know more confidently for animal vs plant primary sources.
source_coverage_notes:
Seven Wikipedia source URLs combine to support the universe + per-vitamin food-source values. One vitamin-universe anchor ('Vitamin' article) + 6 per-vitamin articles (A, B12, C, D, E, K). Each per-vitamin article serves dual roles for its 5 staged rows: (a) discipline-membership universe anchor (which foods count as 'sources of [Vitamin X]' per Wikipedia), and (b) value source (food name + content + source-type label). No per-food articles are cited because the per-vitamin articles already contain the food names and content values for the staged rows; if a future audit requires per-food citation for richer attribute support, per-food Wikipedia articles can be added in a repair cycle.

Roles:
- source_urls[0] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin): universe. Verbatim: 'In humans there are 13 vitamins: 4 fat-soluble (A, D, E, and K) and 9 water-soluble (8 B vitamins and vitamin C).' The staged 6-vitamin universe is curator-chosen from this 13-vitamin list to span both the fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) and water-soluble (B12 representative + C) classification groups.
- source_urls[1] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_A): universe + value (Vitamin A rows 1-5). Article's Sources section names Cod liver oil (30000 μg RAE/100g), Beef liver (4970-21145 μg RAE/100g), Chicken liver (4296 μg RAE/100g), Sweet potato (957 μg RAE/100g), and Carrot (843 μg RAE/100g) with Source Types (Animal × 3, Plant × 2). Article notes: 'animal sources provide preformed retinol in highly bioavailable forms, while plant sources deliver provitamin A carotenoids that require conversion by the body.'
- source_urls[2] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_B12): universe + value (Vitamin B12 rows 1-5). Article does NOT include a numeric food-content table (special case noted in temporal_note + decision_log); the staged content cells preserve the article's qualitative descriptors. Verbatim: 'Animal-derived food sources with a high concentration of vitamin B12 include liver and other organ meats from lamb, veal, beef, and turkey; also shellfish and crab meat'; 'fortified breakfast cereals' as fortified source. The 5 staged B12 rows after cycle-1 audit fix are now article-verbatim: Beef liver, Lamb liver, Turkey liver, Crab meat, and Fortified breakfast cereal — all explicitly named in the article quote. Cycle-0 staged Clams (subspecific to 'shellfish') and Salmon (subspecific to 'fish') with bioavailability percentages misused as content; cycle-1 audit replaced these with the article-named animal organ meats (Lamb liver, Turkey liver) and removed the bioavailability-as-content cell.
- source_urls[3] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_C): universe + value (Vitamin C rows 1-5). Article's plant-sources table names Kakadu plum (1000-5300 mg/100g), Camu camu (2800 mg/100g), Acerola (1677 mg/100g), Indian gooseberry (445 mg/100g), and Rose hip (426 mg/100g). Article notes: 'animal-sourced foods do not generally provide much vitamin C', so all 5 staged C rows are Plant.
- source_urls[4] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_D): universe + value (Vitamin D rows 1-5). Article uses per-serving rather than per-100g content reporting: Rainbow trout (645 IU per 3 oz), Sockeye salmon (570 IU per 3 oz), UV-exposed mushrooms (366 IU per 1/2 cup), Fortified plant milk (100-144 IU per cup), and Fortified cow milk 2% (120 IU per cup). Article notes: 'Few foods naturally contain vitamin D' — fortified sources dominate.
- source_urls[5] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_E): universe + value (Vitamin E rows 1-5). Article's food-composition table names plant oils as the highest-content sources: Wheat germ oil (150 mg/100g), Hazelnut oil (47 mg/100g), Sunflower oil (41.1 mg/100g), Almond oil (39.2 mg/100g), Safflower oil (34.1 mg/100g). Article notes: 'gamma-tocopherol is the most common form found in the North American diet, but alpha-tocopherol is the most biologically active'; animal products provide substantially lower amounts (fish 1.0-2.8 mg/100g).
- source_urls[6] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_K): universe + value (Vitamin K rows 1-5). Article gives both K2 sources (Nattō 1103 μg/100g 90% MK-7; Egg yolk 32 μg/100g; Goose 31; Butter 15; Hard cheese 8-10) and K1 sources from a separate leafy-greens table reporting per-serving units (Collard greens boiled 1/2 cup: 530 μg; Spinach boiled 1/2 cup: 445 μg; Kale raw 1 cup: 82 μg). After cycle-1 audit fix, the 5 staged K rows span both K1 and K2 forms (cycle-0 was K2-only, which the auditor flagged because the partition framing is broad 'Vitamin K' not 'Vitamin K2'): Nattō (K2 fermented), Collard greens (K1 plant), Spinach (K1 plant), Kale (K1 plant), Egg yolk (K2 animal). Cycle-1 dropped the cycle-0 K2 picks Goose / Butter / Hard cheese in favor of K1 leafy greens to honor the broad-K partition framing.

Validation note: each row's Food / Approximate Content / Source Type value is traceable to its vitamin's Wikipedia article. The Vitamin B12 article does not provide numeric content values; the 5 B12 rows preserve the article's qualitative language with a 'qualitative' tag in the Approximate Content cell. Unit variation across vitamins (mg/100g, μg/100g, μg RAE/100g, IU/serving) is preserved because each unit reflects the article's reporting convention; the Approximate Content column is typed 'text' to accommodate this variation.

Universe-size sanity: 6 vitamins is a curator-chosen partition shape from the Wikipedia 'Vitamin' article's 13-vitamin classification (4 fat-soluble + 9 water-soluble; the staged 6 = all 4 fat-soluble + 1 B-complex representative + Vitamin C). 5 foods per vitamin matches the seed-stipulated partition shape (after the cycle-0 expansion from the seed's '3 dishes high in vitamin C' to 'five food sources per vitamin'); total 30 rows.
decision_log:
Candidate card (Stage 1 pre-gate, then Stage 2 scored axes per instance_selection_priorities.md):
- Pre-gate verdict: PASS with three documented risks. R1: '5 most influential / top 5 dishes' is curator selection across multiple vitamins, not source-defined ranking — applied the cycles 1+2+3 lessons upfront by reframing as 'five notable food sources' (selection framing) and using PK = (Vitamin, Food) with List Position non-key numeric. R2: Vitamin B12 article does not provide numeric food-content values — qualitative content cells are used for the 5 B12 rows; documented in normalization_decisions and source_coverage_notes. R3: unit variation across vitamins (mg, μg, μg RAE, IU per various serving sizes) — Approximate Content is typed 'text' to accommodate; per-row units preserve each article's reporting convention. 30 rows >> the 10-row floor; 5-column shape with 1 partition key + 1 list-position ordinal + 1 entity key + 2 non-key text/categorical attributes; strong confidence gradient; LLM-knowable for major nutrition pairings; low temporal sensitivity (vitamin biochemistry stable, content values may shift slightly as USDA / Wikipedia updates).
- Seed/provenance: ADAPTED / EXPANDED from seed #4 in example_questions.txt (line 17). The seed says 'top 3 dishes high in vitamin C' (3 rows, would fail the 10-row viability gate). Cycle-0 expanded to 6 vitamins × 5 food sources to cross the viability gate, exercise multi-vitamin calibration, and apply the cycles 1+2+3 lessons. The seed's word 'dishes' was changed to 'food sources' because Wikipedia per-vitamin articles list ingredients / source foods rather than prepared dishes; documented as a curator choice.
- Category: scaled_enumeration — primary because the instance is a per-partition selection (5 food sources per vitamin) over a partitioned universe (6 vitamins) with multiple non-key attributes. Cycle-0 staged 'top_k' as a secondary category, but cycle-1 audit suggested dropping it because the staged framing is 'notable' (selection) not 'top-K ranked', and the K (mixed K1+K2 with no single ranking criterion) and B12 (qualitative) partitions are not clean top-K rankings. Cycle-1 fix: secondary_category is now empty. The (Vitamin, Food) PK and union+filter operation_type follow the precedent of films / world-religions / decade-inventions / scientists scaled_enumeration instances.
- Source plan: 7 Wikipedia URLs across 1 vitamin-universe anchor (Vitamin) and 6 per-vitamin articles. Each per-vitamin article serves both as discipline-membership universe (which foods are listed as sources of that vitamin) and value source (food + content + source-type). Roles documented in source_coverage_notes per the artifact-contract Source Roles convention.
- Expected shape: 6 x 5 = 30 rows x 5 cols, composite PK (Vitamin, Food). Realized: 30 x 5, 0 duplicates.
- Domain: Food/Nutrition — NEW family per domain_taxonomy.md (Food was unrepresented before this instance; it joins Religion, Technology, Religion as the 4th NEW family added in this session).
- Risks/adaptation: per the three pre-gate risks above. Additional minor risks: (a) the 6-vitamin universe is curator-chosen from a wider 13-vitamin classification — the 8 B-vitamins (B1, B2, B3, B5, B6, B7, B9) are not staged; B12 represents the B-complex. Documented as a future-expansion candidate. (b) Some food sources have alternative names (Acerola = West Indian cherry; Nattō has distinct K1-equivalent representations) — staged values use the Wikipedia article's primary phrasing. (c) Vitamin D content uses per-serving units rather than per-100g because the article reports per-serving — an LLM under test answering with per-100g equivalents should be accepted as semantically equivalent.
- Decision: STAGE.

Further decisions:
1) Per-vitamin 5-food-source selection: (A/C/E) the 5 highest-content food sources per the Wikipedia article's content table; (K) cycle-1 picks span K1 leafy greens (Collard greens, Spinach, Kale) and K2 sources (Nattō fermented + Egg yolk animal) — see audit_response.cycle_1 for the K1+K2 rebalance from cycle-0's K2-only framing; (D) picks span animal (trout, salmon), plant (UV-exposed mushrooms), and fortified (plant milk, cow milk) source types since the article states 'few foods naturally contain vitamin D' and fortified sources are emphasized; (B12) article-verbatim foods from the qualitative source list (organ meats from lamb / beef / turkey + crab meat + fortified breakfast cereals).
2) Schema: composite PK is (Vitamin, Food) with List Position typed 'numeric' (non-key). This applies the cycle-2 lesson from world_religions_top5_holy_sites and twentieth_century_decade_inventions and scientific_disciplines — for selected-not-ranked partitioned tables, the entity column should be the load-bearing key rather than the list-position ordinal. Food names are unique within and across vitamins in this dataset (verified at preflight): no food appears in more than one vitamin-partition.
3) List Position values (1-5 per vitamin) record the curator's documented display order. For A/C/E (where the article gives a single ranked content table): descending content; position 1 is the highest-content source. For D and K (mixed serving-units / mixed K1+K2): roughly content-descending where comparable, with the highest single source at position 1 (Nattō for K, Trout for D). For B12 (qualitative): article-emphasis order (Beef liver position 1 since cited as primary organ-meat source).
4) Approximate Content column: typed 'text' to accommodate unit variation across vitamins (mg/100g, μg/100g, μg RAE/100g, IU/serving) and the qualitative B12 cells. Source-faithful per-row content preservation: each cell reflects the per-vitamin article's reporting convention. An LLM under test answering with normalized per-100g values where the source uses per-serving (Vitamin D) should be accepted as semantically equivalent.
5) Source Type column ('Animal' / 'Plant' / 'Fortified' / 'Fermented'): typed 'categorical' because there are exactly 4 distinct values across the 30 rows. Source Type is article-supported per row and provides a categorical attribute beyond the numeric content for calibration.
6) Vitamin B12 qualitative-content special case: the Vitamin B12 Wikipedia article does NOT include a numeric food-content table (verified by direct fetch of the article). After cycle-1 audit fix, the 5 B12 rows preserve the article's verbatim food-name list (Beef liver, Lamb liver, Turkey liver, Crab meat, Fortified breakfast cereal — all named in the article's 'organ meats from lamb, veal, beef, and turkey; also shellfish and crab meat' and 'fortified breakfast cereals' phrasings) with content cells uniformly tagged 'qualitative; article cites...'. Cycle-0 had misused the article's fish-bioavailability metric as a content cell for one row; cycle-1 audit flagged this and the cell was removed when Salmon was replaced with Turkey liver. An alternative would be to drop B12 from the universe (giving 5 vitamins × 5 = 25 rows) but that would lose B-complex representation; or to supplement B12 numeric content from per-food Wikipedia articles (e.g., Beef liver article gives ~70 μg/100g for B12) — could be a future repair cycle if audit requires.
7) Vitamin name format uses 'Vitamin X' with explicit 'Vitamin' prefix matching Wikipedia article-title conventions (Vitamin A, Vitamin B12, Vitamin C, etc.). Single-letter form ('A', 'C') would be ambiguous.
8) Unit choice per vitamin follows the per-vitamin article's reporting convention: A/C/E/K use mg or μg per 100g; A specifically uses μg RAE (Retinol Activity Equivalents) which is the modern Wikipedia convention; D uses IU per serving (the article's reporting convention given fortification emphasis). Consistency across vitamins was sacrificed for source-fidelity.
normalization_decisions: Vitamin names use the 'Vitamin X' Wikipedia article-title form (Vitamin A, Vitamin B12, Vitamin C, Vitamin D, Vitamin E, Vitamin K) — single-letter form ('A', 'C') would be ambiguous. Food names use Wikipedia article-title form or the article's primary phrasing where the article gives one (Cod liver oil, Beef liver (cooked), Sweet potato (baked), Kakadu plum, Camu camu, Acerola, Sockeye salmon (cooked), Nattō (fermented soybeans), Wheat germ oil). Approximate Content column: typed 'text' to accommodate per-vitamin unit variation (mg/100g for C/E, μg/100g for K, μg RAE/100g for A, IU per serving for D, qualitative for B12). Source-faithful per-row formatting; each cell reflects the per-vitamin article's reporting convention. For Vitamin B12 (no numeric table in the article), content cells preserve the article's qualitative descriptors quoting the 'high concentration of vitamin B12' phrasing with a 'qualitative; article cites...' tag (cycle-1 audit fix removed an earlier misuse of an article bioavailability percentage as a content value). Source Type column ('Animal' / 'Plant' / 'Fortified' / 'Fermented'): 4 distinct categorical values; 'Fermented' is used only for Nattō (Vitamin K row 1) which the article describes as a fermented K2 source distinct from Animal or Plant. List Position is a 1-5 within-vitamin ordinal recording the curator's documented display order (per-vitamin rationale: descending content where article ranks numerically; article-emphasis order for B12). Sort order is (Vitamin ASC, List Position ASC).
open_questions: 1) The Food family target is 5 instances per instance_selection_priorities.md; this is the first. Future Food instances could include 'major cuisines x 5 signature dishes' (cuisine taxonomy) or 'macronutrient sources x 5 foods' (carbohydrate, protein, fat splits) or 'culinary-acid sources x dishes' (vinegar, citrus, fermented). 2) The 6-vitamin universe is curator-chosen from a wider 13-vitamin classification. The 8 B-vitamins (B1, B2, B3, B5, B6, B7, B9) are not staged; B12 is the B-complex representative. A future expansion could add Folate (B9) or Niacin (B3) which are widely cited in nutrition. 3) Vitamin B12 qualitative-content cells are a documented special case. Two alternatives: (a) drop B12 from the universe → 25 rows, 5 vitamins, all numeric; (b) supplement B12 content from per-food Wikipedia articles → adds ~5 more source URLs and shifts to partially_supplemented if the supplements override the source-defined content. The cycle-0 staging accepts the qualitative B12 cells as honestly source-defined-from-the-cited-vitamin-article. 4) Unit variation across vitamins (mg vs μg vs IU; per-100g vs per-serving) is preserved per the source's reporting convention. An audit could push for normalized units (e.g., always per-100g, always μg) — that would require unit conversion the cited articles do not directly support and is not done at cycle 0. 5) Vitamin D rows use per-serving units (3 oz fish, 1/2 cup mushrooms, 1 cup milk) rather than per-100g because the article reports per-serving. An LLM under test giving per-100g equivalents would be defensible. 6) Some foods are cooked/preparation-specific (Beef liver cooked vs raw, Carrot frozen/cooked, Sockeye salmon cooked, UV-exposed mushrooms). The article qualifies these forms; the staged rows preserve the qualifier. An LLM answering with the un-qualified food name should be accepted as semantically equivalent. 7) Source Type 'Fermented' is used only for Nattō. An alternative would be to merge Fermented into Plant (Nattō is fermented soybeans, plant-base) or to add more fermented foods (kimchi, tempeh, sauerkraut) — the 4-category taxonomy is what the cited articles support without curator interpretation. 8) Acerola is also called 'West Indian cherry' or 'Barbados cherry'; the staged value uses 'Acerola' per the Vitamin C article's primary phrasing. 9) The seed asks for 'dishes' but the Wikipedia per-vitamin articles list ingredients / source foods rather than prepared dishes — the staged column is 'Food' not 'Dish' to match what the source provides; documented as a curator choice.

blocking_addressed: B12 row support: cycle-0 staged Clams (subspecific to article's 'shellfish' phrasing) and Salmon (subspecific to article's 'fish, fowl, and meat' phrasing) and used the article's 40-60% bioavailability metric for Salmon's content cell, which is bioavailability not content. Cycle-1 fix: replaced Clams and Salmon with Lamb liver and Turkey liver — both explicitly named in the Vitamin B12 article quote 'liver and other organ meats from lamb, veal, beef, and turkey'. The 5 staged B12 rows are now article-verbatim (Beef liver, Lamb liver, Turkey liver, Crab meat, Fortified breakfast cereal) and all 5 content cells are uniformly qualitative descriptors quoting the article's 'high concentration' phrasing without misusing bioavailability percentages.

K rows K2-only -> K1+K2 mix: cycle-0 staged 5 K2-rich foods (Nattō MK-7, Egg yolk K2, Goose K2, Butter K2, Hard cheese K2), but the partition was framed as broad 'Vitamin K' which encompasses both K1 (phylloquinone, leafy-green dominated) and K2 (menaquinone, animal-and-fermented dominated). The cycle-1 audit flagged this as a partition-scope mismatch. Cycle-1 fix: rebalanced K rows to span K1+K2 — Nattō (K2 fermented, highest content) + Collard greens (K1 plant, 530 μg per 1/2 cup boiled) + Spinach (K1 plant, 445 μg per 1/2 cup boiled) + Kale (K1 plant, 82 μg per 1 cup raw) + Egg yolk (K2 animal, 32 μg per 100 g). Dropped cycle-0 K rows: Goose meat, Butter, Hard cheese (all K2-only). The Approximate Content cells now flag K1 vs K2 form per row (e.g., '1103 μg per 100 g (K2 / MK-7)', '530 μg per 1/2 cup (K1)').

Cycle-1 audit suggested revisiting because the staged title is 'notable' (selection framing) and the B12 + K partitions are not clean top-K rankings (B12 is qualitative, K is mixed K1+K2 with no single ranking criterion). Cycle-1 fix: dropped secondary_category to '' to honestly reflect that this is a scaled_enumeration partitioned-selection without a top-K ranking claim.
